subject: gnomeTinkerer
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: gnome tinkerer with a backpack of gadgets.
Style: whimsical low-poly mix.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the structure of a TypeScript module for a gnome tinkerer character, roughly 0.9-1.1 meters tall with a backpack of gadgets, keeping the model manageable while being careful about correct SDK usage since I can't test it directly. I'm working out the skeleton proportions, starting with hip placement and building up from there.

I'm figuring out the joint and chain hierarchy — hips as root, then spine joints up to chest, neck, head, and jaw, with arms and legs handled as separate chains using limb roles. For the body shapes, I'm planning to attach chunky rigid primitives to each joint for that stylized puppet look.

For the torso, I'm using a sweep along a spine chain with varying radii to shape a pear-like silhouette, feeding in points from hips up through the chest to the neck. I'm also sketching out a texture plan — eyes, goggle lenses, a gauge, patches, belt buckle, hat stripes, and a blueprint scroll — plus a glow effect for the lantern.

I'm sketching the character parts now: boots with toe caps, striped sock-legs, and a tinkerer gnome outfit with a teal tunic, leather apron, and a deep red-orange hat banded with brass gears.

For the belt, I'm considering using a loop sweep around the torso's spine joint, but weighing whether a lathe-built ring might be safer than relying on the loop surface matching the torso's varying radius -- ultimately deciding to trust the loop approach.

I'm deciding to keep the torso as a single rigid lathe piece attached to the spine/chest joint, shaped like a tunic from hem to shoulders, with a separate pelvis/hip skirt piece if needed, rather than overcomplicating with bendy segments.

Now I'm nailing down actual height measurements: feet at y=0, boots 0.10 tall, legs short with hip/knee/ankle joints, torso spanning roughly 0.30 to 0.74, neck, then a big rounded gnome head topped with a tall cone hat. I'm weighing whether to scale everything down since real garden gnomes are small, maybe shrinking the whole figure to stay proportional and believable.

I can import a gearTrain from the clockwork kit path separately from the main SDK exports, which should be allowed. I'll place the gear train on the backpack's back face, facing outward so it's visible from behind the character.

Now I'm working out the gear positions and spacing so they mesh properly without overlapping non-adjacent gears, calculating distances between gear centers based on tooth counts and module size to confirm the layout holds together.

I'm shrinking the gear module to fit within the backpack face bounds, recalculating pitch and tooth counts for both gears so their extents stay within ±0.15, then checking joint naming for the spin animation to make sure they're unique.

Now I'm placing a gauge cylinder and texture plane on the pack's +X-facing side with the rim oriented along that axis, while double-checking that the backpack's width doesn't collide with the arms hanging at the torso's sides.

For the arms, I want a slight T-ish rest pose with elbows bent back, so I'm computing shoulder-to-hand distances to make sure the reach stays within the limb's max length, adjusting the hand target position so it doesn't overstretch.

For hands, I'm considering giving each hand a small fist sphere plus separate finger structures built as joint chains so a rigger would recognize them properly, rather than rigid attached rods, weighing the added complexity against anatomical realism.

Still writing finger geometry...

I'll skip giving the hand a held tool since they're meant to be open and relaxed, putting any tools like a wrench on the belt or backpack instead. Now I'm working out the head structure—a skull sphere plus a separate lower jaw wedge, with a gnome-style bulbous nose.

For facial features, I want goggles pushed up onto the hat brim with glowing lenses, small beady black eyes with highlight decals, and a bushy white beard and mustache covering most of the lower face. The jaw needs to be a skin-colored wedge hidden under the beard so it can articulate independently, with the mustache resting over the lip and a small mouth gap peeking through below it.

Now I'm building the skull as a sphere with pointed gnome ears as sideways cones, rosy cheek spheres, a large tomato-colored nose bump, and eye textures decaled precisely onto the curved skull surface using position and direction vectors to seat them correctly.

For the eyes themselves, I'm sketching a simple symmetrical SVG design: a white sclera ellipse, dark iris, and small highlight dot, paired with bushy brows. Then I'm thinking through goggles for the hat using brass rim shapes with a glowing lens center.

Still writing goggle code...

I'm working out hat placement against the head geometry — positioning the band low on the forehead with the rim radius matched to the skull curvature at each height, tilting it back slightly, then noting the eye level for the next feature.

Now I'm plotting the sweep path for the pointed hat cone, curving it upward and backward to a curled tip above the head.

For the surface treatment, I'm adding a gold bell at the tip, striped patchwork texture along the hat body, and a decal emblem on the front face, since decals can target a sweep surface directly. Next I'm working out the hat brim geometry where it meets the head.

Checking that the cuff radii overlap properly with the cone, then adding brass studs around the hat using a ring arrangement — spacing ten spheres radially so they stick outward along each frame's facing axis.

Since ring callbacks don't pass a bone, I'll explicitly set bone: head on each stick. For the goggles, I'm positioning them on the front of the hat where it curves forward, estimating the cone radius at that height to place the lens center around z≈0.145 so they sit flush against the surface.

Now I'm working out the strap: a closed loop of 12 points around the hat's circumference at roughly radius 0.14, swept with a thin leather tube so it wraps naturally around the cone's curve.

I need to make sure the sleeve cuff and strap don't collide positionally, then decide on sweep facet settings — using low facet counts for a faceted low-poly look rather than smooth shading, and applying painted stripe textures along the sweep's length. Now I'm turning to the beard, which needs to feel like the character's signature feature — building it as a layered teardrop-shaped base with additional blade-like strands for texture, giving it a braided gnome-like quality.

Working out the beard's sweep geometry: a flattened elliptical cross-section that tapers as it falls from chin to chest, positioned so it extends forward of the torso and overlaps the neck and shoulder area naturally without clipping through the tunic.

Setting up the extrude axes so the beard lock outlines draw in the front-facing plane, with thickness extending forward in Z.

I work out the local orientation vectors so the thickness direction points forward and up along the beard slope, computing the cross product to confirm it aligns correctly. I'll build a helper function for creating individual locks with position, length, width, angle, and color parameters.

I'll implement this using applyAxisAngle on the normal vector to get the rotated frame. The beard is rigged to the jaw bone so it opens with the mouth, which is realistic since the sweep starts near the mouth. For the mustache, I'm planning two curling bezier sweeps from under the nose outward, tapering in radius and attached to the head bone.

Now I'm computing the sphere surface position at each mustache control point so the strands sit flush against the head rather than floating or clipping into it, adjusting z-depth by adding a small offset to the computed surface radius.

Then I'm planning the nose as a protruding bulb sphere placed slightly forward from the head surface with mottled coloring, and figuring out symmetric eye placement as decals on the skull surface.

Now I'm working out bushy white eyebrow curves above the eyes and shaping pointed ears as side-facing leaf extrusions, considering whether to use cones or flattened extruded outlines for a more natural ear shape.

Still refining ear orientation...

Switching to the neck piece as a short skinned cylinder connecting torso to head joint, then starting the torso's lathe profile for the tunic shape.

Shoulders sit around y=.60 with radius .13, so I'll position arm joints slightly outside at (±.15,.57,0) with rounded sphere shoulder pads for sleeves. For the belt, I'll trace a loop on the torso surface near y=.37 with a slight lift, then sweep a thin tube along that path using default upward direction.

For front details like the buckle, buttons, and pocket, I'm casting a ray from the front toward the torso to find the exact placement point, handling the case where it might return null. For the apron, I'm considering draping a flat extruded plate against the curved front rather than building a full lathe shape.

Now I'm working out suspender straps draping from the belt up and over each shoulder to the back, using box-sectioned sweeps with flattened rectangular cross-sections, and these same straps will double as the carrying straps for a pack.

For the front, I'm considering a bib or apron plate that sits flush against the curved torso surface, calculating where a flat rectangular plate would intersect the torso's radius at different heights so its edges follow the body's curvature rather than floating off it.

Rather than physical geometry, I decide it's simpler to just paint the bib region directly onto the torso using a function that checks position and colors it differently from the tunic, giving the look of overalls without added mesh complexity. I also plan a shading helper that mixes warm and cool tones based on surface normal direction to fake cel-style lighting on the torso.

Mapping out the arm sweeps next—plain tunic color for the upper arm, skin for the hand, and a cuff band near the wrist using a distance-based color swap for the brass bracelet accent.

I'll use a nested paint function that switches between cuff and tunic colors based on distance to the wrist point, letting paints resolve recursively. For the legs, I'm setting up the hip-knee-ankle chain with limb geometry where the hip-to-ankle distance is short enough that the knee naturally bends forward.

With the three-name chain, the extra name gives the chain a tip joint at the ankle, so I'll add parts like boots onto that tip and consider adding a separate toe joint for a boot cap. For the pants, I'm planning a mustard-brown sweep color with sock stripes layered underneath.

Still designing leg sweep bands and boot geometry...

Adding a cylindrical boot shaft and cuff fold at the ankle, keeping sole bottoms resting at y=0. Now I'm planning the backpack as a child joint off the chest, sketching its main frame box dimensions and position so it embeds slightly into the torso's back for a seamless attachment.

I'm fleshing out the backpack details: a mottled olive-brown canvas body with riveted brass corner brackets, a darker leather top lid with hanging buckle straps, a red-pink bedroll lashed across the top with spiral rope bands, and a gauge on one side with a brass telescope tube angled out the other.

The telescope itself gets three tapering segments with brass end rings and a glowing lens tip, holstered diagonally near the hat so it tucks just below the hat's curled brim. For the back, I'm planning a visible gear train near the central clock mechanism.

Up top, I'm adding a small rotor mast with a hub and two thin blade extrusions, and I'm figuring out a copper pipe with a coiled section using the kit's sweep/coil helper.

Now I'm placing a copper tank cylinder on the left side of the pack, checking clearances against the arm and shoulder so nothing collides, then working out the full side-by-side component layout for the pack's left and right faces.

Adding pressure gauge and steam pipe...

On the right side I'm adding a telescope in a holster plus a hanging lantern with an amber glow, mounted on a bracket rod extending from the pack with a chain down to a hexagonal cage lantern, checking it clears the arm's swing.

For the back face I'm placing gears and a crank centered up top, with dangling tools (wrench, bell, spoon, hammer) hung from cords off the lid for character. On top I'm adding a bedroll, rotor mast, and a glowing jar of green liquid with cork and bubbles plus a few small glowing crystals for magic flavor.

Now I'm adding glowing cyan goggle lenses and a tiny glowing gear brooch to the gnome's hat and head, then working out the base: a circular wooden platform sized to just slightly exceed the gnome's arm-spread footprint, sitting flush so the lowest points touch floor level at y=0.

I need to figure out how to offset the whole model upward by the base's thickness so the gnome stands on top rather than sinking into it -- simplest is building the base from y=-0.05 to 0 and keeping the gnome's feet at y=0, then grouping everything under a single root object.

Rather than threading an offset through every coordinate, I could just design the base as a thin disc sitting flush at y=0, but that risks violating the rule that nothing should sink below the floor beyond the small tolerance. I need a cleaner way to guarantee the lowest point rests exactly at y=0 without littering every call site with manual adjustments.

I'll keep the sole resting at y=0 with the thin disc base dropping just 0.022 below, and add a raised lip ring around the edge for visual depth. I also want to scatter story props near the base—mushrooms, a small gear-clock, a toolbox beside the gnome—to give it more character.

For the arrangement I'm thinking toadstools tucked back-left, a tiny mechanical cog-beetle on the right side, and a crate with a blueprint scroll at the back-right, leaving the front clear. I'm placing a wooden crate stack near x=0.45, z=0.15 on the left side.

Given the scope, I should aim for roughly 600+ lines of careful code rather than max length, since quality matters more than hitting a target. Now I'm cataloging what's actually exported from the SDK's math and color modules — things like vec, mix, noise, paint, rgb, smoothstep, and resolve — so I know what to import for computing vectors and blending colors, and confirming that paint functions can return raw RGB tuples as valid color input.

Thinking through type safety next: I'll define a simple 3-number tuple type for positions rather than relying on SDK point types, and I'm deciding to always pass an explicit bone reference when placing parts at literal coordinates rather than letting the builder guess which joint is closest, since that auto-assignment seems error-prone.
